Science & Technology
• A widespread Microsoft outage continued to disrupt Outlook, Teams, Microsoft 365 and Copilot worldwide, with the company saying there’s no sign of a cyberattack and reporting uneven recovery across regions as governments and public services scrambled with contingencies.
• Policy and space headlines: Nvidia privately told a US lawmaker chip-tracking to curb smuggling is technically feasible, while SpaceX targets a “double-catch” Starship test and ULA’s Vulcan returns to flight; ESA’s Euclid issued its first major data release; researchers reported an AI proof limiting certain quantum-computing advantages and a first robot-assembled structure in space.
Why it matters: The outage underscores systemic dependence on a few cloud providers, while chip-tracking, space milestones, and fundamental research advances will shape technology governance, industry security, and future infrastructure.

• Nvidia’s leadership scandal widened into Washington, with Democrats launching a probe into China sales and Commerce Secretary Lutnick set to testify; Moscow told Europe to designate an envoy to join talks.
Why it matters: Flashpoints from Iran to Ukraine intersect with great-power diplomacy and tech-security scandals, testing cohesion among allies and the credibility of emerging peace frameworks.

Entertainment.title: Culture Over Couture: Why Luxury is Doubling Down on Streetwear
Entertainment.text: To understand why European luxury fashion houses are frantically reverting to "buzzy" logos, viral collaborations, and streetwear architects, we have to look past the runway and into the balance sheets. The recent game of creative director musical chairs, which saw Martine Rose appointed as Balenciaga's new creative director following Pierpaolo Piccioli's brief 16 months stint, is not just a shift in aesthetic taste—it is a defensive maneuver against a severe macroeconomic reality.People are simply not buying luxury like they used to. In 2026 alone, Europe’s top luxury conglomerates had roughly $350 billion USD wiped from their market value amid a prolonged spending slowdown, heavily driven by a pullback in the Chinese market and the evaporation of aspirational shoppers. When consumption power plummets, quiet luxury doesn't pay the bills; brands need massive cultural noise to stimulate a stagnant market.The Attention Economy: Instant Cool Over Quiet HeritageThis economic reality is compounded by a fundamental shift in how technology has rewired our consumption behavior. With infinite information at our fingertips, consumer attention spans have been severely fractured by the algorithmic churn of TikTok and Instagram. In this hyper-connected ecosystem, trends live and die at breakneck speeds, and the traditional six-month fashion calendar feels painfully slow to a consumer conditioned by the feed. Today's audience is perpetually chasing "the cool"—and they demand it immediately.Consequently, traditional brand "heritage" is losing its standalone currency. Heritage demands patience; it requires the consumer to appreciate the slow, quiet romance of archival history and artisanal craft. But in a digital landscape dominated by visual noise, quiet gets scrolled past. "Instant cool"—a subversive logo flip, an unexpected sneaker drop, or a viral celebrity co-sign—registers in a microsecond. To keep a chronically bored, easily distracted audience interested, luxury brands must provide a relentless dopamine hit of novelty. They are no longer just competing with other fashion houses; they are competing for screen time against the entire internet.The Kering Conundrum: Gucci, Balenciaga, and the Hype BlueprintTo understand the financial urgency driving these creative decisions, look at Kering. The conglomerate has been struggling profoundly, largely due to consistent sales drops at its flagship cash-cow, Gucci. When Gucci recently attempted to pivot away from maximalist hype toward a quieter, more elevated minimalism, the market response was lukewarm.Kering knows exactly what works when the chips are down, because they’ve done it before. During his tenure at Balenciaga, Demna practically invented the modern luxury-hype playbook. His influence even spilled over into Kering’s other crown jewel when he partnered with Gucci’s then-director Alessandro Michele for the 2021 "Hacker Project." By cross-pollinating Balenciaga and Gucci logos, they treated heritage luxury houses like streetwear drops, breaking the internet and driving massive sales.This economic and cultural pressure perfectly explains the recent whiplash at Balenciaga. Pierpaolo Piccioli, a master couturier and traditionalist, was brought in to elevate the house. Yet, he was ousted after just 16 months. While his tailoring is impeccable, a struggling Kering cannot afford a quiet, slow-burn couture revival. They need the viral, algorithm-breaking revenue engine that defined Demna’s era.By bringing in Martine Rose—who consulted under Demna and has deep roots in London’s rave, hip-hop, and Jamaican-British communities—Balenciaga is returning to the well of hype. Though Rose is formally trained and has the eye of a sculptor, her tailored, slightly skewed normcore aesthetic possesses the exact street-level cultural cachet Kering needs to force consumers to stop scrolling, open their wallets, and offset Gucci's slump.The faces driving the modern luxury survival strategy are no longer just traditional dressmakers. Designers like Martine Rose (now at Balenciaga) and NIGO (Kenzo) bring deeply ingrained subcultural roots to heritage houses. Pop-culture titans like Pharrell Williams treat Louis Vuitton as a cultural broadcasting network, following the collaborative blueprint laid by Kim Jones. Meanwhile, Grace Wales Bonner is proving that the future of luxury—soon to be seen at Hermès—requires a masterclass in both Savile Row tailoring and street-level hype.LVMH's Pop-Culture Blueprint: NIGO, Pharrell and Kim JonesLVMH anticipated this cultural necessity years ago, effectively transforming its heritage houses into global pop-culture broadcasting networks. When LVMH appointed NIGO—the undisputed godfather of global streetwear and founder of BAPE—as the Artistic Director of Kenzo, it was a seismic validation of the culture. It proved that streetwear pioneers were no longer just seasonal collaborators; they were the safest bet to drive sustained youth engagement and volume.This blueprint was drawn by Kim Jones. At Louis Vuitton, Jones orchestrated the landmark Supreme collaboration, officially breaking the dam between skate culture and high fashion. At Dior Men, he built a collaborative engine, bringing in Matthew M. Williams of 1017 ALYX 9SM for industrial hardware. To execute these cultural crossovers, Jones relied heavily on his lead footwear designer, Thibo Denis, who masterminded the Dior x Air Jordan 1—a release that perfectly bridged Parisian elegance with ravenous sneakerhead obsession.The success of that formula is precisely why Denis recently ended his six-year run at Dior to join Louis Vuitton, teaming up with Pharrell Williams. Pharrell’s succession of the late Virgil Abloh at LV proves that in a tough economy, a creative director must be a cultural curator first and a traditional dressmaker second.The Hermès Reality CheckIf you want proof of how pervasive this economic chill is, look at Hermès. Traditionally the quietest, most insulated ultra-luxury house—buoyed by the artificial scarcity of the Birkin and a clientele of ultra-high-net-worth individuals—Hermès is often immune to inflation. But even they are feeling the shift in consumption power. While their core leather goods division kept the brand in the green for Q3 2026, their ready-to-wear and accessories division actually dropped by 2% amid weak demand in China.This context makes their upcoming January 2027 menswear debut under Grace Wales Bonner so crucial. Wales Bonner perfectly encapsulates the modern luxury requirement: she possesses profound historical research and Savile Row-level tailoring skills, but she also boasts unimpeachable "streetwear chops," having single-handedly dictated global footwear trends with her adidas Samba collaborations. Hermès knows that to move ready-to-wear in 2027, they need a designer fluent in both high-end craft and street-level hype.Blurring the Line or Erasing It?What does this mean for the definition of luxury? It means the line between luxury and streetwear has not just been blurred; it has been entirely erased by economic necessity.In a booming economy, luxury houses can afford to sell the romance of quiet exclusivity and heritage craftsmanship. But in a global slowdown where consumers are fiercely protective of their disposable income, luxury must fight for attention. Streetwear—with its drop models, high-profile collaborations, and ingrained cultural community—is no longer just a trend infiltrating the runway. It is the financial lifeline keeping the luxury industry afloat.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Vans and Pringle of Scotland Wrap Three Premium Icons in Fuzzy Argyle Wool
Entertainment.text: Name: Vans x Pringle of Scotland CollectionMSRP: $110 - $130 USDRelease Date: Available NowWhere to Buy: VansVans and Pringle of Scotland have joined forces on a winter collection that combines Southern California skate culture with more than two centuries of Scottish knitwear heritage.At the heart of the footwear-led lineup are three of Vans’ Premium icons: the Authentic 44, the Sk8-Hi Reissue 38 and the Classic Slip-On 98. Each is dressed in Pringle’s signature argyle, rendered in brushed and felted wool rather than canvas. Underneath, the shoes keep their Premium upgrades: padded collars and uppers, a refined footbed with a Sola Foam ADC insole for all-day cushioning, taller sidewalls with a glossy finish, foxing tape inspired by Vans’ reinforced outsoles from the ’90s, and the brand’s signature waffle tread.The collection comes in two main color schemes, each applied as a patchwork of argyle and harlequin-diamond panels rather than a single repeating pattern. “Navy/Marshmallow White,” found on the Classic Slip-On and Sk8-Hi, mixes navy, burgundy, olive and sage green, with thin cream lines crossing the larger diamonds and a sage-and-navy checkered panel wrapping the toe.The Sk8-Hi adds navy suede overlays at the toe, eyestay and heel, along with a tonal navy Sidestripe and matching laces. “Black/Marshmallow White,” available on the Authentic and a second Classic Slip-On, takes a sharper approach, combining black, white and blush-pink diamonds, with black collar binding and white laces on the Authentic.Every pair sits on a glossy "Marshmallow White sidewall with a contrasting foxing stripe. Co-branded “Vans x Pringle” labels appear on the tongues of the lace-up models, and campaign images show Pringle’s lion rampant embroidered on the heel quarter above the classic “Off The Wall” heel tab, with a gum waffle outsole underneath.Part of a braoder collection, the accompanying apparel and accessories range includes heavily patterned cardigans, knit shorts, sweater vests, track sets, beanies, socks and tote bags, all utilizing the same luxurious knitwear techniques and colorways seen across the sneakers.Set your reminders and get ahead of what’s dropping next on Hypebeast Drops.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: doublet Turns Your Most Used Emojis Into a Bag for FW26
Entertainment.text: Summarydoublet’s FW26 "EMOJI LEATHER BAG" features 3D cowhide emoji expressions.The design physicalizes unseen human emotions to lighten emotional weight.It releases November 9 for approx. $860 USD at select retailers.Masayuki Ino’s doublet has always thrived on humor and subversion, turning the mundane into the unexpected. For its Fall/Winter 2026 collection, the brand taps into everyday emojis and turns them into something you can wear with the EMOJI LEATHER BAG.The playful design stems from a longstanding adage: bags that look like faces sell well. doublet took the saying literally, utilizing intricate leather patching and precise stitching to recreate three emoji expressions in three dimensions across the front of the bags. The available expressions include the crying-laughing face, the pleading face, and the green vomiting face.Crafted from soft cowhide leather, the tote balances its loud exterior with practical, everyday utility. Equipped with a detachable shoulder strap, allowing the wearer to effortlessly switch between hand-carry and crossbody styling.Beyond its immediate visual punchline, the design carries a deeper meaning. doublet finds that human emotions are inherently invisible. The brand wants to explore how, by boldly wearing these unseen feelings as a physical object, the wearer could reduce the emotional weight they carry and make them feel lighter.Available in Camel and Black, the doublet EMOJI LEATHER BAG releases on November 9, available for ¥137,500 JPY (approx. $860 USD) at doublet’s online store, and select retailers in Japan.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: EVISU x FAF x BEAMS T Remix ’90s Archival Denim Across a Five-Piece Debut Collection
Entertainment.text: SummaryEVISU, FAF and BEAMS T have joined forces for the first time on a five-piece collection built from EVISU’s 1990s denim archiveFAF reinterprets archival EVISU cuts and motifs through its design focus on clothing that moves between urban and outdoor lifeJapanese rapper MIKADO produced an original track for the launch and will perform it live at a party in HarajukuEVISU, FAF and BEAMS T have unveiled their first joint collection, a tight five-piece lineup that pulls EVISU’s archival denim into the present with updated cuts and reworked graphic details. FAF leads the design side, revisiting silhouettes and decorations from EVISU’s 1990s heritage and adapting them for wearers who split their time between the city and the outdoors. The result is a capsule spanning denim, fleece and accessories, all anchored in the craftsmanship that built EVISU’s reputation.The denim jacket and jeans form the backbone of the collection, each refitted with cuts drawn from reinterpreted archival patterns rather than lifted wholesale from the vault. EVISU’s signature seagull logo makes its return here too, now rendered in sequins for a glinting take on one of Japanese denim’s most recognizable marks. Together, the pieces read as a faithful nod to the label’s early output, sharpened with proportions that suit a contemporary wardrobe.Moving beyond denim, the zip-up hoodie carries EVISU’s original “Ishigaki Camouflage” pattern, giving an in-house print a fresh canvas outside the brand’s usual five-pocket territory. The graphic sweatshirt takes a more playful route, merging EVISU and FAF iconography and characters into a single design that makes the partnership visible at a glance. Both pieces lean into the collaborative premise, pairing one label’s archive with the other’s graphic sensibility.The shoulder bag is the collection’s most literal homage, shaped as a trompe l’oeil of EVISU’s denim back pockets. By turning the brand’s most identifiable denim detail into a standalone accessory, FAF lets the archive function as both reference point and object. It rounds out a capsule where every piece traces directly back to a specific EVISU signature.Music forms the final layer of the project. MIKADO produced an original track for the occasion and will perform it at the launch party at BEAMS T Harajuku on November 20 from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. JST, with DJ sets from Tokyo-based VLOT and other local acts filling out the bill.The EVISU x FAF x BEAMS T collection arrives on November 20 at EVISU Japan and BEAMS stores. Online, it drops at 12:30 p.m. JST via EVISU JP, BEAMS and ZOZOTOWN, and at 6:30 p.m. JST via EVISU US. A wider rollout follows on November 21, when the collection lands in-store and online in Taiwan, Hong Kong and the US.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: ‘GTA VII’ Outside America? Rockstar Won’t Rule It Out
Entertainment.text: SummaryRockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson has declined to rule out a ‘Grand Theft Auto’ game set outside the US, though he stopped short of confirming any plansThe comments land as ‘GTA VI’ prepares to launch with what is described as the series’ most detailed recreation of America to dateRockstar has weighed overseas settings before, with a shelved ‘GTA: Tokyo’ concept and pitches spanning Rio de Janeiro, Moscow, Istanbul, London and ParisGrand Theft Auto may not be bound to American soil forever, with Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson signaling that an international setting remains possible for the franchise. Speaking with The Guardian ahead of GTA VI’s launch, Nelson was asked whether Rockstar could picture a mainline entry outside the US. His answer left room for it, though he did not reference a specific sequel or commit to any destination.Nelson’s full response was brief and carefully balanced. “Never say never, but there’s still so much to do in America,” he told The Guardian. The line keeps the series’ home turf firmly in focus while acknowledging that a departure is not off limits. Any talk of a GTA VII setting remains speculation, since Rockstar has yet to formally announce a follow-up.The scale of what Rockstar builds helps explain the caution. GTA VI returns players to Vice City, the studio’s fictional stand-in for Miami, and expands outward into the surrounding state of Leonida. The game has spent more than a decade in development and is billed as the franchise’s most detailed take on America yet, which sets an enormous bar for any city Rockstar might attempt next. Recreating a foreign capital at that fidelity would mean rebuilding street-level cultural knowledge, signage, traffic patterns and local character from scratch rather than iterating on familiar ground. Leonida itself is modeled on Florida.That familiar ground has defined the series for decades. Liberty City, Los Santos and Vice City have rotated through the franchise as satirical mirrors of New York, Los Angeles and Miami. Each return has let Rockstar layer new technology onto a known blueprint. The series has technically left the US once before, with the 1999 expansion Grand Theft Auto: London 1969 taking the top-down original to British streets.Behind the scenes, Rockstar has entertained bigger overseas swings. Former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij has said a GTA: Tokyo project was seriously considered at one point, with a Japanese developer possibly leading production. He has also pointed to Rio de Janeiro, Moscow, Istanbul, London and Paris as locations that were discussed internally, though none advanced into a finished game.For now, Rockstar’s attention stays on Leonida, with GTA VI launching on November 19.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Theaster Gates Recasts Tar, Clay and Gym Floors for His Hong Kong Exhibition ‘Surrogate’
Art & Culture.text: SummaryTheaster Gates revisits his signature motifs in ‘Surrogate,’ transferring them onto new materials or setting them in fresh compositionsThe show includes fire-hose imprints in clay, reclaimed gymnasium flooring, a clay “handbag” and a trio of new Tar PaintingsThe exhibition explores how art can stand in for something absent, whether a family bond, a community or a history that has been overlookedTheaster Gates brings Surrogate, an exhibition of new works, to Gagosian Hong Kong from November 19. The show finds the Chicago-based artist mining his own visual language, lifting elements from earlier series and reworking them through different materials and arrangements. Each piece is built on the idea that an artwork can act on behalf of something that isn’t there, a thread that has run through Gates’ practice for more than a decade.Fire hoses offer the clearest example of that material shift. Gates has used decommissioned hoses since 2011 in his Civil Tapestries, flat, striped compositions that call up the hoses turned on civil rights protesters. For Surrogate, he presses those same hoses into slabs of clay, so the ridged texture once read as fabric and paint now sits in fired ceramic surfaces.A similar reworking happens with his “gym floor” pieces, a series he started in 2014 using varnished planks salvaged from school gymnasiums. Rather than leaving the court lines in their original layout, Gates has reorganized the painted markings into graphic bands. The new geometry echoes a set of paintings he made in the late 2010s, which drew on the data visualizations of Black life that sociologist W. E. B. Du Bois and his students produced in 1900.The exhibition’s clay “handbag” moves the conversation from flat surfaces to form. A handbag is useful and also signals taste and identity, and Gates uses it to extend his long-running interest in vessels, from ceramic pots to buildings, as objects that hold and protect what is placed inside them. The piece also connects to ritual practices such as ikebana, where the container is part of the act itself.Rounding out the show is a trio of new Tar Paintings, a series Gates began in 2011. Each is assembled from layered panels of industrial roofing sheets, the same kind of material that featured in his 2022 installation at London’s Serpentine Galleries. Their hard-edged compositions recall geometric abstraction and Minimalism, but the medium is personal, drawn from the trade of Gates’ father, a professional roofer. This latest group also introduces symbolic marks for the first time, including the Chinese character for “vista,” which points to an open view of a real or imagined landscape.Gates’ use of materials as stand-ins extends well beyond this show. For “Documenta 13,” he used salvaged parts of an abandoned Chicago building to bring Huguenot House in Kassel, Germany, back into use. Elsewhere, he has drawn on historic archives to push back against the erasure of Black people from the record. Visitors to the region can see more of his work in Seoul, where Gates is concurrently showing African Still Life at White Cube Seoul through December 18.Surrogate opens at Gagosian Hong Kong on November 19 and runs through February 27, 2027.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
